Explainer · Coastal science

Why the tide is late

High water should follow the moon. In most harbours it trails it by hours, and the reason is the shape of the sea floor.

Every schoolchild learns that the moon pulls the oceans into a bulge, and that the Earth turns beneath it. That picture predicts two high tides a day, each arriving about fifty minutes later than the last. It gets the rhythm right. It gets the timing wrong almost everywhere.

The moon sets the beat

The lunar day is 24 hours and 50 minutes. Gravity from the moon, and to a lesser degree the sun, raises a force that varies smoothly over that period. What the ocean does with that beat depends on the instrument it is played on.

Every basin has a note of its own

A body of water sloshes at a natural period set by its length and depth. When that period is close to the lunar half-day, the basin resonates and the tide grows enormous: the Bay of Fundy's natural period is about 13 hours, so a modest push becomes a 16-metre range.

The ocean is not a puddle following the moon. It is a set of bells, each struck twice a day.

A tide is a wave thousands of kilometres long, and in shallow water such a wave travels at a speed set by depth alone. Crossing a shelf to reach a port takes hours, and every hour of travel is an hour of lag.
